name: Stenström technique

lead: The Stenström technique shapes a prominent ear by scoring or rasping the front of the cartilage so it bends back into a natural fold. It dates to 1963 and remains in use, especially in France.
Published results are surgical case series reporting high correction and satisfaction rates.

paras: Abrading the antihelical cartilage weakens one side so the cartilage curves toward the intact side, recreating the missing fold.
General otoplasty complications include hematoma, infection, suture extrusion, asymmetry and overcorrection. Controlled trials are not available.

lead: The Stenström technique (Stenström otoplasty) is an ear-pinning procedure in which the front surface of the antihelical cartilage is scored or rasped so that the cartilage bends backward and forms a fold. It was described by Sten Stenström in 1963.[1][2][3]

It is used for prominent ears caused by a failure of the antihelix to fold. Wikipedia describes the principle as weakening the cartilage on one side so it curves toward the intact side.[2] Surgeons in France are reported to use it widely, and modified versions are published.[4][5]
Evidence consists of surgical series and technique papers; published satisfaction and effectiveness figures come from case series, not controlled trials.
infobox: Anterior abrasion of antihelical cartilage so it folds[2]

paras: In Stenström's method the cartilage surface at the antihelix is abraded or scored, which releases the tension that holds the cartilage flat and lets it curl into a fold.[2] Grokipedia describes it as perichondrial scoring followed by posterior suturing, later adapted to a fully posterior approach.[3] A 2016 technical note describes introducing the rasp by an anterior approach as a refinement.[5]
Stenström published his technique in 1963, the same year as Mustardé's suture method.[2][3] A 1978 article in Clinics in Plastic Surgery is titled The Stenstrom otoplasty.[1]

An Italian report on indications for surgery stated that Stenström otoplasty and/or suturing the concha to the mastoid periosteum was effective in 95 percent of the authors' cases.[4] A 2024 study from a Saudi military hospital reviewed results and patient satisfaction with a modified Stenström technique.[6] General otoplasty complications listed by Wikipedia include hematoma, infection, suture extrusion and overcorrection.[2]

Published studies are retrospective or descriptive. They include the 1993 Italian experience reporting 95 percent effectiveness,[4] the 2016 technical refinement paper,[5] and the 2024 Cureus study of modified Stenström otoplasty and patient satisfaction.[6] No randomized trials were found.
